claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) triggers automatic checkpointing after a commit when the WAL contains at least N frames.
claims.quote: causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: An N value of zero or less disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: New connections enable automatic checkpointing with a default threshold of 1000 pages or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT.
claims.quote: Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

claims.text: Automatic checkpoints use PASSIVE mode.
claims.quote: All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.

claims.text: Continuously overlapping readers can prevent checkpoint completion and cause unbounded WAL growth.
claims.quote: if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Attempting checkpoints during reader gaps can avoid starvation.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: The default checkpoint runs in the thread performing the COMMIT that crosses the WAL size limit.
claims.quote: By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.

claims.text: Checkpoint-triggering COMMIT operations can be much slower than other COMMIT operations.
claims.quote: This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.

claims.text: Infrequent checkpoints amortize checkpoint cost across more writes.
claims.quote: To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible, meaning that one wants to run checkpoints infrequently

claims.text: Regular checkpointing helps maintain read performance by limiting WAL size.
claims.quote: Hence, to maintain good read performance it is important to keep the WAL file size down by running checkpoints at regular intervals.

claims.text: Failure to obtain the checkpoint lock because another process is checkpointing returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy handler.
claims.quote: If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

claims.text: If the busy handler returns zero while obtaining the writer lock or waiting for readers, checkpointing falls back to PASSIVE behavior.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE

claims.text: The busy-handler fallback returns SQLITE_BUSY even though it may checkpoint some frames.
claims.quote: checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

claims.text: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage before checkpoint content moves into the database.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database

claims.text: The database file must be synced before the WAL is reset.
claims.quote: the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL. Checkpoint also requires more seeking.

claims.text: Writers sync the WAL on every commit with PRAGMA synchronous=FULL but omit that commit sync with NORMAL.
claims.quote: Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.

claims.text: With PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL, checkpointing is the only operation that issues an I/O barrier or sync.
claims.quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers to finish.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback.
claims.quote: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL waits until there is no writer and all readers use the most recent snapshot.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot.

claims.text: While FULL is pending, it blocks new writers but allows new readers.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: After checkpointing, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART waits until all readers read only from the database file, ensuring the next writer restarts the log.
claims.quote: after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE adds zero-byte log truncation immediately before a successful return to RESTART behavior.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP checkpoints zero frames and exposes pnLog and pnCkpt counters.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: pnCkpt includes frames checkpointed before the current function call.
claims.quote: the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)

claims.text: The writer can rewind the WAL when it has all been transferred and synced and no readers use it.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: Ordinary checkpoint recycling overwrites the WAL from the beginning rather than normally truncating it.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: A reader's end mark stays fixed throughout its transaction, preserving a single point-in-time view.
claims.quote: for any particular reader, the end mark is unchanged for the duration of the transaction, thus ensuring that a single read transaction only sees the database content as it existed at a single point in time.

claims.text: A checkpoint must stop at a WAL page beyond any current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: Configuring automatic checkpointing replaces an existing sqlite3_wal_hook callback.
claims.quote: The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook() .

claims.text: Registering sqlite3_wal_hook disables automatic checkpointing configured through sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint.
claims.quote: Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: A NULL or empty zDb attempts the operation on all attached WAL databases and leaves output counters undefined.
claims.quote: If parameter zDb is NULL or points to a zero length string, then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db. In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.

claims.text: SQLITE_BUSY on an attached WAL database does not stop attempts on the remaining attached databases.
claims.quote: If an SQLITE_BUSY error is encountered when processing one or more of the attached WAL databases, the operation is still attempted on any remaining attached databases and SQLITE_BUSY is returned at the end.

claims.text: The shared-memory wal-index helps readers locate WAL pages with minimal I/O.
claims.quote: a data structure called the "wal-index" is maintained in shared memory which helps readers locate pages in the WAL quickly and with a minimum of I/O.

claims.text: The wal-index shared-memory requirement confines readers to the same machine and prevents this WAL implementation from working on a network filesystem.
claims.quote: the use of shared memory means that all readers must exist on the same machine. This is why the write-ahead log implementation will not work on a network filesystem.

claims.text: Rollback journaling saves original database content in a separate journal before writing changes directly into the database.
claims.quote: The traditional rollback journal works by writing a copy of the original unchanged database content into a separate rollback journal file and then writing changes directly into the database file.

limitations: Scores are selection judgments using the supplied rubric; Rel/Use/Nov/Int/Via denotes relevance, usefulness, novelty, interest, and viability, and the research threshold is 3.2.
No tools or scoring validator were run; scores were calculated directly for this bounded test.
The inventory contains only SQLite, transactions, and write-ahead logging; their presence does not establish coverage of the narrower concepts listed here.

The supported parent neighborhood is already represented by the inventory, so no missing parent concept is asserted; rollback journaling is a sibling of WAL at that parent level rather than a checkpoint mode.
The packet supplies no evidence establishing an emerging frontier within the last 12–18 months, so no frontier concept is manufactured.
All sources originate from SQLite; viability scores reflect useful but uneven packet coverage, not satisfaction of independent-source requirements for full research.
S1 describes three checkpoint subtypes and mentions RESET, while S2 explicitly documents PASSIVE, FULL, RESTART, TRUNCATE, and NOOP; no separate RESET mode is inferred.
S1 warns that RESTART and TRUNCATE might block readers, whereas S2 says RESTART does not impede readers; the packet does not resolve this difference.
No unsupported historical explanation or disagreement resolution is inferred.
RESEARCH marks viable gaps, not completed downstream research; one extraction pass and its 36/36 new-information rate do not demonstrate saturation.
